cards.note: Sugarcane plantations are very common in Northern Queensland, due to its tropical climate.

cards.a: Car Meta - Gen 3; Red Car; Long Antenna
cards.note: A red Generation 3 car with a long antenna can be seen in and east of Melbourne.
The town of Gascoyne Junction in Western Australia is distinct, as the driver left the car boot open while covering this town, creating a very unique car meta.

Australia is home to dozens of rare Google cars, which can usually be found in natural reserves.

Most rare Google cars with snorkels are located in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. The only snorkel cars outside of NSW are in the northwestern part of Wunaamin Conservation Area (northern WA) and along Lucky Bay (south coastal WA).
On most of the Northern Territory section of the Barkly Highway and a small part of the Queensland section, a wire can be seen on the left side of the car.
In some of New South Wales’ Generation 2, the halo looks very dirty. This is most common west of ACT and south of Barrington Tops.
Generation 2 coverage cannot be found in Northern Territory. It can also help in 50/50s between Victoria and Tasmania, where Gen 2 is more common in Tasmania.
In Generation 2 coverage in an area of Eastern NSW, a twig is visible in the Generation 2 halo.

In a lot of Generation 2 around the towns of Morwell and Traralgon in Eastern Victoria, an entire leaf is visible in the Generation 2 halo. A version with only the top half of a leaf can also be seen in eastern SA.
The upper half of a leaf can sometimes be seen on the Generation 2 halo in southeastern South Australia. If it's an entire leaf, it is in Eastern Victoria.
Jervis Bay only has Gen 1 coverage, all of which has a 2021 copyright.
Around the Devils Marbles, north of Davenport in the Northern Territory, smoke from a bushfire is visible.
A sun with "splodges" around it can be observed on the 95 in Western Australia, between Newman and Ex Doolgunna.
The ∀-Poletop is found in South Australia and New South Wales. In SA, the pole will be a stobie pole, while in NSW it will be round.
Within Australia, a speed limit of 130 km/h can only be found in the Northern Territory.
South Australia is the only Australian state that uses a 25 speed limit in school zones.
Poletops in Tasmania often consist of a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees to form an L-shape.
Unique to Australian Capital Territory (Canberra).

These black markings are specific to electricity poles in Queensland. They are often accompanied by diagonal numbers.

They are almost exclusively found between Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast
These black-and-white stripy bollards are unique to Western Australia.
This black-and-yellow bollard is exclusive to Queensland.
Melbourne poles commonly feature these white, rectangular stickers, with a smaller blue square inside it.
Bollards with brown paint at the bottom are most commonly found in Western Australia.
Reflectors that are shorter than the regular ones are most common in Queensland and South Australia.
Identified by the little symbol.
Roads that start with the letter ‘C’ are only found in Victoria and Tasmania. In addition, South Australia has some C roads near the border with Victoria.

As a general rule in Queensland state, Australia, red tinted roads are found mostly around Charters Towers (especially when you have more trees), they can also be found on the A2 near label, and the 1 further north. These areas are indicated in the distribution, but there may be minor exceptions.
According to a 2006 review, 64% of all concrete poles are located in the state of Victoria.
The city of Darwin, NT uses concrete shelters as bus stops.
Dorat Road (23) in the Northern Territory can be easily recognized thanks to its distinct Darwin area landscape and lack of road lines.
These round concrete poles with dots going up on them are found in New South Wales.
Some signposts in South Australia and Western Australia are flat rather than round.
Road signs with a fluorescent border are almost exclusively found in Queensland.
This street sign is unique to Gold Coast City Council.
This Green Dot on poles is sometimes found in New South Wales.
Poles in Western Australia often have green painted bases, and sometimes a white sticker or a red and white band attached.
You can find these dark green property markers on the sides of roads in Western Australia.
These poles with hanging insulators are found in Queensland and New South Wales.
You can find these white hydrant poles that feature a blue circle and a red section on top of it in Victoria.
These fire hydrants with red painted tops are unique to Victoria.
Very slim license plate (similar to Swiss front plates) are found in Victoria and New South Wales. While in Victoria, you can usually see two blue blocks of texts, in NSW they appear plain.
Very slim license plate (similar to Swiss front plates) are found in Victoria and New South Wales. While in Victoria, you can usually see two blue blocks of texts, in NSW they appear plain.
Blue plates on Taxis are found exclusively in New South Wales.

All-yellow road lines can be seen on roads around Mount Kosciuszko.

In addition, a unique white truck with a snorkel, and cab guard can be found.
The white ‘No Stopping’ and ‘No Parking’ signs that include text are unique to the Australian Capital Territory.
New South Wales uses these two designs for bus stops. One is blue and has a white B in a circle with it, the other has the signpost bending over the actual sign.
This guardrail ending, featuring a black dash on a yellow background, is almost exclusive to New South Wales and the ACT.
License Plates in Northern Territory have bright red lettering which shines through the blur. Looks kind of similar to the Queensland plates, which are a bit darker.
Octagonal Poles in Australia are found mostly in and around Sydney.
Olive-green possum guards are only found on electricity poles in Tasmania.
The 'H' poletag is found in New South Wales.
This poletag with 'HP' is found in New South Wales.
Within New South Wales, purely horizontal poletags (i.e. no vertical on the same pole), are not found around Sydney.
In NSW, poletags in the triangle formed by Sydney, Newcastle and Scone (view map) almost always have one or two letters in their codes.

cards.a: Infrastructure - Poletag - NSW - Vertical / Outer White
cards.note: Within NSW, these vertical plates with white ends are not found near Sydney. Note that otherwise, vertical plates will be close to Sydney within NSW.
Poletags with a blue sticker, and a vertical steel tag are found in Queensland, north of Rockhampton.

Within NSW, regular vertical poletags are found south and west of Sydney.

Note that if the poletags have white ends on each side, they are NOT close to Sydney, but rather throughout the rest of NSW.
This poletag which consists of rectangular yellow stickers that usually form a T, is exclusive to New South Wales.
Bus stops in Queensland have a yellow signpost bending over the actual sign.

The Queensland License Plate has dark red letters which can shine through the blur. Looks similar to the NT plate, which has a lighter red tone. There is also an old, green version, which could theoretically show up.
Queensland features these unique pole tops with coils that are angled upwards on the sides.
Circular blue stickers can be found on Queensland poles. You may occasionally see the same type of sticker in a different colour, or with the colour almost completely faded.
New South Wales is the only state to use red ‘No Stopping’ signs.

cards.a: Infrastructure - Roadline Gap with no Reflector
cards.note: In South Australia and the ACT, you can sometimes find gaps in the outer roadlines. If this gap has no reflector, it is South Australia.
In South Australia and the ACT, you can sometimes find gaps in the outer roadlines. In ACT, there will always be a reflector in the gap. This can also appear occasionally in South Australia.
These rusty metal poles, containing several holes, are unique to the Northern Territory, and rarely the northern part of Western Australia.
Signposts in the Northern Territory can feature these yellow stickers.
You can sometimes see sloped kerbs in Perth, where it gradually declines to the road, whilst in other cities kerbs go straight down at a 90 degree angle.
Orange signpost, sign extending over the signpost.
The iconic Stobie pole, made of steel and concrete, is specific to South Australia. Outside of SA, it sometimes occurs in Broken Hill, NSW or Tasmania.
This street sign is unique to the City of Sydney.
Different versions, but usually have "Metro" written on them.
Some ‘Keep Left’ signs in New South Wales, Queensland, and the Northern Territory use this thinner version, which does not include an arrow.

cards.a: Infrastructure - traffic light with no outline
cards.note: Traffic lights without a border are found in Northern Territory, South Australia and Victoria.

cards.a: Infrastructure - traffic light with white outline
cards.note: Traffic lights with a white outline around the frame are found in the eastern and western states of WA, QLD, NSW, ACT and Tas. Traffic lights without a border are found in the remaining, central states.
The Sturt Highway from Wentworth to Wagga Wagga can have triple broken centre lines. They can also be found on other major roads in NSW, such as the Gwydir Highway.
A trident-like pole top with the insulators pointing to the top can sometimes be seen in Western Australia and Victoria.
Bus Stops in Victoria can be recognized by their color scheme: White-Orange-Black-Grey-White.
License plates in Victoria have a little small triangle at the top, which can sometimes be recognized through the blur.
Victorian pole tops feature 3 circular coils; 2 on the sides, and 1 vertical one at the top. At times, other extensions can be seen on these poles.
Bus Stops in Australia are marked by these horizontal poles with information on them.
Western Australian License Plate have blue letters and a thin blue stripe at the top, which can sometimes be recognized through the blur.
White directional signs can only be found in Tasmania.
You can find these white property markers on the sides of roads in South Australia.

Yellow license plates can occasionally be found in New South Wales. Most license plates are still white, though. The old design of Western Australian plates is also yellow, so you might stumble upon them in WA very rarely.
Yellow signposts are specific to Western Australia.
Poletops that resemble the cyrillic letter ш are unique to South Australia.
Alice Springs, an isolated town in the southern part of the Northern Territory, features distinct orange rocks that can be seen in the distance or at the end of roads.
The northern QLD city of Cairns is distinct due to its tropical vegetation and big green mountains around the city.
The vegetation in the area surrounding Darwin is extremely distinct. It features dark red soil, as well as rich green grass and trees. The tree trunks are typically black.

The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has quite dry vegetation and is made up of shrubs and wide cronwed eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a white tint.

Western South Australia has a similar landscape, but with orangish soil.

Lush green or golden fields can be found in this band from the south of the Yorke Peninsula to Echuca. In the SA side, the landscape should be drier than the Victorian side and more wide crowned eucalyptus can be seen. On the Victorian side, the trees generally have more leaves and are taller.

cards.a: Landscape - Inland New South Wales Landscape
cards.note: The landscape in inland NSW is mostly flat, and the soil gets redder the more inland you go. Vegetation consists of mostly dry pale-green shrubs. Further east and on the Queensland and Victorian borders, the climate gets more temperate but is still quite dry and more eucalyptus trees can be seen, with the soil transitioning into a more sandy colour as well as more hills being visible.

Kangaroo Island in South Australia tends to have a distinct look. The vegetation mostly consists of bushes and low, stubby eucalyptus trees with puffy clusters of leaves. The orange soil colour is reminiscent of Western Australia.

In addition, the island only has Generation 2 and Generation 4 coverage, with Generation 2 being most common.
The area around Mount Gambier, SA features white soil and extensive pine tree plantations, making it recognisable.
Coastal northern Queensland is very tropical. Typical vegetation consists of palm trees and dark green vegetation.

The Nullarbor Highway (Latin for “no tree”) can be easily recognized thanks to the flatness, overall grey look and very low vegetation.

NOTE: Use the road angle or road lines to determine whether you are on the WA or SA side.
Western Australia, and especially the Perth area, is known for its reddish-orange soil.

cards.a: Landscape - Stuart Highway with Blue Car
cards.note: The Stuart Highway from Alice Springs to around Pimba, SA can be easily recognized by its bright orange dirt, short trees and blue car Generation 4.

Tasmania has a cool temperate climate which is uncommon in the rest of Australia and is comparable to central-southern Chile or New Zealand. Typical landscape consists of green rolling hills that can look dry in winter coverage. Eucalyptus trees can be seen on the side of roads and on hills in the distance. Rural Tasmania is also quite hilly with dense eucalyptus forests making up the landscape.
Termite mounds can sometimes be seen in the Northern Territory and rarely northern WA and QLD. They appear as brown, spiky formations rising out of the ground.
The area around Tom Price can be recognized by its red soil and rocky hills.

The area around Warramboo in SA to Madura in WA has a unique landscape. Vegetation is quite dry and is made up of shrubs and wide crowned eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a slight orange tint.

The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has a similar landscape, with the same vegetation but usually with whiter soil.
While Bottle Trees can be found throughout Queensland, they are planted everywhere in the city of Roma.
These brush plants are commonly seen in Western Australia.

Excoecaria parvifolia is an odd looking tree with almost creepy looking thin vine outgrowths as leaves. It seems to be found primarily found around the new 2025 white car coverage around the northern Queensland city of Gregory, Australia.
The Queensland fan palm or Australian fan palm, is a species endemic to northeastern Queensland, Australia (Specially around Cairns).
The sand palm is endemic to the north of the Northern Territory of Australia, from the Fitzmaurice River to Cape Arnhem and inland as far as Katherine.
